question.problem:
Solve the modular equation $3x≡5\,(\text{mod}\,14),$ expressing your answer as a nonnegative integer smaller than $14.$

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*

$x≡$
{{field-1}}$\,(\text{mod}\,14)$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=3$ and $n=14$, and

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(3,14)=1.
$$

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $3\,(\text{mod}\,14).$ To find the inverse of $3\,(\text{mod}\,14)$, we compute the exponents of $3\,(\text{mod}\,14)$ until we get a result of $1\,(\text{mod}\,14):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{3} & ≡9\cdot 3≡27≡13 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{4} & ≡13\cdot 3≡39≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{5} & ≡11\cdot 3≡33≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ {3}^{6} & ≡5\cdot 3≡15≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,14)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $5\cdot 3≡1\,(\text{mod}\,14),$ which means that $5$ is the multiplicative inverse of $3$ (modulo $14$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ 5\cdot 3x & ≡5\cdot 5 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ (5\cdot 3)x & ≡25 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡1\cdot 14+11 &  & (\text{mod}\,14) \\ x & ≡11 &  & (\text{mod}\,14)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡11\,(\text{mod}\,14).$
